analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour, starting about three months after enactment.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee in January 2021, drew no cosponsors, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to set the federal minimum wage at $15 an hour, up from $7.25. Unlike most minimum wage proposals, it would not phase the increase in over several years — the new wage floor would take effect on the first day of the third month after the bill became law. The bill never advanced beyond being referred to the House Education and Labor Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers currently paid at or near the $7.25 federal minimum wage would get roughly a doubling of their hourly pay within months of enactment. Workers earning somewhat above $15 could also see raises if employers adjust pay scales upward, and states without their own minimum wage would see the biggest change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minimum wage workers in low-wage states

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 6(a)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act to require employers to pay at least $15 an hour, up from the $7.25 in effect since 2009.
Sets the effective date at the first day of the third month after enactment, so the full increase would arrive quickly rather than being phased in over years.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay at or near the current federal minimum — restaurants, retail stores, hotels, farms, and other low-wage businesses — would bear higher labor costs. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through higher prices, and employers in lower-wage regions and territories would face the largest adjustments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: The increase takes effect in about three months with no phase-in period, which is much faster than most minimum wage proposals; even supporters of a $15 floor have typically favored multi-year schedules to give small employers and low-wage regions time to adjust.

A single national $15 floor applies the same wage to Puerto Rico, American Samoa, the Virgin Islands, and other territories whose wage levels are far below the mainland's, which is why minimum wage bills usually include special schedules for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Roughly doubling the wage floor for the country's lowest-paid workers is a large, direct benefit to them, and the cost falls on a scattered group of employers rather than on the workers themselves. The main honest objection is design, not intent: a no-phase-in jump to $15 within three months, applied uniformly to the territories, is faster and flatter than the schedules most economists and even most $15 advocates have endorsed, raising the risk of job losses or reduced hours in the lowest-wage areas.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Living Wage Now Act on January 15, 2021.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day, and that was the last action the bill ever received.
No other member cosponsored the bill at any point in the two-year Congress.
The bill never reached a committee vote, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate.
Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so any future minimum wage increase would have to start over in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the $7.25 federal minimum wage kept the status quo, since no wage increase was enacted in the 117th Congress. Workers paid $7.25 gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no markup, no vote, no report — during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and House majority leadership, 117th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, which was typical treatment for member-introduced minimum wage bills that leadership chose not to prioritize.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors beyond its Democratic sponsor, so the partisan shape of a potential floor fight never showed itself.

industries.note: The bill would roughly double the wage they must pay their lowest-earning workers within about three months, raising their labor costs. Those costs are the same dollars that become paychecks for minimum wage workers, so the industry's interest runs against the bill's benefit to workers.
